utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Good morning. I see that there's a videolink with Belgrade. Could the representative of the Registry in Belgrade tell me who is present in the room where he is at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] Myself, Andre Sabbah, to my right is Velibor Ostojic, and to my left is Richard Hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No other persons present, I take it?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] No other persons present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. Sabbah.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I didn't get any sound.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I notice that the volume should be adjusted now and then. If someone is a native -- is speaking English, then it should be louder so that we get the original, and if we are receiving what is said in another language translated into English, then the volume should go down a bit so in order not to obstruct hearing the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can hear you perfectly well, Your Honour. Could I just have a test in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Sabbah, could you speak a few more words?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [In Belgrade] Yes, Your Honour, we are in Belgrade with --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, no problems?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I haven't got a LiveNote. I'm going to try and log on to this computer. The Court can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Mr. Ostojic, good morning. Mr. Ostojic, I'd like to remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you've given at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I heard "dobro jutro," but I didn't get any translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ostojic, I'd like to draw your attention to paragraph 42 of your witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You stated that you do not remember the government forming teams of ministers for on-site investigations. I would like to show you the minutes from the government meeting of the 24th of May, 1992 in your language, and I would like to read out a portion of that to you. And for the parties it's P65, tab 139. Have you found the minutes of the government meeting of the 24th of May in your material, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to -- I now have some interference, but ... First of all, looking at these minutes, do they refresh your memory about whether government ministers were sent to the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember, despite the document, that I was ever sent to on-site visits pursuant to the conclusions reached at this meeting of the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I take it that you found the relevant portion where these minutes read: "It has been concluded that the overall situation in the republic should be recorded as soon as possible. To that end, groups of ministers would be formed which would conduct on-site investigations in municipalities and would prepare the reports and would suggest the measures to be undertaken." That doesn't change your recollection, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can only assume that item 4 referred to my duties with regard to the printing press that should have been put in place, if I had any tasks at all. As for me being sent somewhere pursuant to the conclusions of this session, I really can't remember, and that is all I can say in response to your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, this Court has received evidence that you were sent on such a mission to Vogosca and Ilijas on the 29th of May, 1992. I would like to show you the minutes from the government meeting of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina of the 29th of May. For the parties it's P65, tab 140. You find it in the binder in your language as well. And on page -- the second page it reads: "Milan Trbojevic and Velibor Ostojic are responsible for the visits to the municipalities of Vogosca and Ilijas, while Nedeljko Lajic and Ljubomir Zucovic are responsible for the visits to the municipalities of Stari Grad and Centar." And these minutes from which I just quoted also say the following: "In the course of these visits they should talk to the Crisis Staffs, take note of the situation, by all means visit the front, make contact with the soldiers, and prepare a report for the government." Mr. Ostojic, are you able to tell us why the government did decide to send ministers to the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on these minutes, I'm trying to establish, given the fact that I don't remember that I went to Vogosca with Mr. Milan Trbojevic. I believe that this conclusion was never implemented. Maybe Mr. Trbojevic knows better than me because he was the one in charge and he was the vice-president of the government, and he was my superior in the government by virtue of his position. I suppose that the task was to improve the situation on the ground, to remove all -- any deviation that might have existed on the ground, to establish the order, and to establish state institutions on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the second quote I gave very much goes to military matters and not just -- not primarily to establish state institutions. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is what I read in the conclusions in the minutes, but I don't remember and I claim that I was never there, I didn't go there. On page 3, under item 2 of this conclusion, I can read that we were supposed to look into the work of the organisation called Dobrotvor and also what is with the payment transactions and financial control. That is why I believe that it was within the purview of the Vice-President Trbojevic, who was also the vice-president of the state administration at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You answered already my next question, whether you actually went on those missions. At least you said you claim that you did not go and you could not have gone. Is -- is it your recollection that you did not go or do you say: Well, my recollection is such that it doesn't tell me that I went? So therefore is it that you say: I positively state that I never went there? Or do you say: I don't remember that I ever went there? Of course in this time, in this context.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If my memory serves me well, I never went to the front line and I never went to any positions pursuant to this conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you at that time go to these municipalities? Because the visit to the front line was, I would say, part of the job. But did you go to Vogosca and Ilijas in that period of time?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say with a hundred per cent certainty that I wasn't there at the time or before or after; that I wasn't there I can't say with certainty. But I remember that I was never sent to a mission to inspect the front lines in those municipalities. In any case, this was not within the purview of the information minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And meeting the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember this at all. And regardless of that, I really cannot remember ever having attended a meeting of any Crisis Staff, and especially not in the municipality of Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any -- did -- do you have any recollection whether Mr. Trbojevic went or whether Mr. Lajic and Mr. Zucovic went on such missions?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Zucovic, no, no. I simply cannot claim that. It would just not be serious, and I have taken the solemn declaration that I would speak the truth. I don't know whether any of the mentioned ministers ever went to visit the -- these municipalities. Not only do I not remember, but I don't know whether this was ever implemented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to move to another subject. I would like to ask you about detention centres. You said in your witness statement in paragraph 43 that you never visited detention camps. Now, it is alleged that you, Mr. Ostojic, went together with Mr. Bozanic and journalists to tour all the camps. Do you stand by your statement that you never visited detention camps or would you like to add anything to that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by my statement with full responsibility. I never visited a single camp, nor did I have any duties there. Second of all, Mr. Bozanic, I believe that during the period of time that we are talking about, was not physically present in Pale, so there could not have been a physical link between Mr. Bozanic, who was a journalist of TV Sarajevo till the end of May 1992 or maybe until mid-June of that year. I'm really surprised to see the allegation that I went to visit a camp with Mr. Bozanic and some other gentlemen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are now specifying a certain period of time. If you say: "I never visited a single camp" --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, given the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would that be true for the whole of 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, we received testimony which says, and it is about camps, and it relates to August. The question to that witness was: "... when ITN and the Guardian reporter entered the Omarska camp and sent dispatches and videos which were distributed worldwide. You know about that event?" Then the witness answered: "That's not right. Mr. Ostojic took the journalists there, and we have an excerpt from the Kozarski Vjesnik. He said that there was no censorship. His impression was different from the impression gained by the journalists. Also there was this press release of the government stating that what the journalists wrote about is not true." The witness said: "You still have this press release there. You have it here today. That's what I found out. The journalists wrote about it and then a team was sent out to check whether this was true. Commissions were sent out to see whether this was correct. Journalists went together with Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Bozanic to tour all the camps, all of them." Does this refresh your memory as to what happened, most likely in August 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, my memory has not been jogged, but I have my statement in which it says that I did not visit camps and I stand by that. I can also state that this witness's statement is very confusing and it doesn't specify the camps. It just mentions a certain time in August and all camps. This is absolutely incorrect. There is a decision of the government in connection with the questions of the world media about camps in Republika Srpska. Journalists had to be allowed a free access to Republika Srpska and free movement about it, and they had to be given an opportunity to write about these camps and whether they existed or not, whether there was just columns of people withdrawing and retreating from the areas that were struck by war. Not only in August, but throughout the period the Ministry of Information enabled all journalists to move freely through Republika Srpska and to go to any town or any place at their own request, and the Ministry of Information was there to allow them to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What exactly caused the government to respond so extensively on what was published at that time in the world media?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was caused by incorrect information on concentration camps and the false propaganda to the effect that there are camps all over Republika Srpska. That is why the Ministry of Information organised two press conferences; one here in Belgrade, organised by the news agency Tanjug, and another one in Bijeljina that was held in the municipal building. And to these press conferences, all international media wishing to visit Republika Srpska were invited in order to see whether there are any camps indeed in Republika Srpska, as we could read in the reports of some of those media.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Were there many that reported or was it just a minority of the international media that reported on the existence of such camps?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this press conference in Bijeljina that I held, because I was assigned to by the government of Republika Srpska, there were many, in my estimate over 20, leading international journalists and representatives of electronic and press media. And they were enabled to go in the direction of Banja Luka, Prijedor, Pale, wherever they wished, because the government had decided to task the ministry to allow all journalists to remove all hindrances, and there were no hindrances in the first place, to their travel so that they can see with their own eyes what the situation was with the camps in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, you said in one of your previous answers it was concentration camps was -- the existence of concentration camps was false propaganda. Now, let's just focus, for example, on Omarska camp. Do you still consider this to be false information or -- I mean, did you have the proper information at that time which allowed you to establish that it was false propaganda? Or was it the other way around, that the press was -- international media were better informed and that you did not know exactly what was going on in these camps?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, I have never been there, and one can form the best opinion if one sees for oneself. In that case, you know better than any medium what the truth is, better than if you read it from whatever media. However, that was not my job. My job was to enable journalists to visit every area in Republika Srpska. Second, all the knowledge that I gained from domestic and international reports --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. My question was whether -- at this moment you say: No, I was not correctly informed at that time and the reporting was reflecting the actual situation. Or do you at this moment say: No, they were wrong. It was propaganda. Such camps and the conditions in these camps did not exist as they were published in the international media?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, sorry to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour is asking the witness to give his opinion today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: His opinion today as to whether camps existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So whether -- looking back whether he was then well-informed. So, Mr. Ostojic, what I'm trying to find out is --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is a matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- whether you at this moment still consider that to be false reporting on the situation in the camps.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe it was a pre-planned, well-thought-out propaganda to misrepresent simple refugee columns as concentration camps. I know of a specific medium in Australia that used archive footage from 50 years ago, misrepresenting it as a current camp in Republika Srpska. So I stand by what I said before. As far as I am informed, as far as I remember, and as far as I can form my position, those were not concentration camps. Those were columns of refugees withdrawing from combat-afflicted areas. That is what I said at the said press conferences in 1992 to all the international media who were interested in hearing what I had to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So perhaps let's focus on one of these camps that drew a lot of attention at that time. So you say Omarska was a situation where refugees were withdrawing from combat-afflicted areas. It was not a place where under very poor conditions in terms of food, hygiene, a large number of men were detained, even men which had nothing to do with combat activities. That's -- I just now give a short picture. You say: That is not true, it was just a situation - I don't know whether you had Omarska in mind - where refugees were withdrawing from combat-afflicted areas?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking in general terms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm asking you --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Saying that Republika Srpska did not have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Especially to avoid that we get confused, I give Omarska as one example and ask you whether Omarska would reflect your description that it was just refugees withdrawing from combat-afflicted areas.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I believe. It's another matter whether within that refugee group decent conditions of living were organised. In that respect, I do allow the possibility that the population concerned did not have the proper living conditions, but I stand by my earlier statement that neither Omarska nor any other place was planned as a camp. I am not aware that anyone planned to organise a camp anywhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, you are introducing new elements which are strange to my question. I didn't ask about planning; I asked about whether such camp did exist. And I asked you whether nowadays you still are of the opinion that camps did not exist and, as you said, that it was just about refugees withdrawing from combat-afflicted areas, rather than, as I put it to you, a place where under very poor conditions in terms of food, hygiene, a large number of men were detained; that is, they were kept there and were not allowed to leave.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I will try to focus and to give a succinct answer to your question. I believe to this day that it was not a camp, and I stand by that position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move to another subject. Mr. Ostojic, you also said in your witness statement in paragraph 43 that do not recall a visit to Susica camp in Vlasenica together with members of international organisations in August 1992. Mr. Ostojic, this Court has heard evidence that you visited Susica camp and that you had a conversation with the camp commander about the conditions in the camp. Does this allegation refresh your memory about a visit that you made to Susica camp?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no way I can refresh my memory because that's simply not correct. I adhere to what I said earlier. I am firm in my position that I've never been to Susica. I know where Vlasenica is because I passed through, but I'm not aware of Susica. And I can only add that people may have confused somebody else for me. But I do not understand why I as a minister of information was supposed to deal with humanitarian issues when we had a commissioner for refugees, and we had other institutions that were part of the government that dealt with humanitarian affairs. And I'm simply surprised and confused by the allegation or the finding that I visited that camp. It really takes me by surprise. If you want to know whether I can refresh my memory, I cannot. I don't remember, and I simply haven't been there, regardless of any allegations or statements or testimony by whatever organisation or individual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, do you remember at that time - and still in relation with camps - whether you ever gave a -- whether you had a -- whether you gave an interview to Kozarski Vjesnik?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been as part of the press conference that I held for all the media. As far as Kozarski Vjesnik in particular, I cannot recall talking to them individually because it would have been incredible with such a mass of reporters. Maybe I have talked to all of them at the press conference, and then Kozarski Vjesnik somehow drew on that material to make something look like an interview with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It may be that you said already where this press conference was held. Could you please -- if you said already, could you please repeat it. If not, could you tell us where this press conference was held?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I held two press conferences concerning the organisation of visits by all media to Republika Srpska regarding that problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My question was where these press conferences were held.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Belgrade and Bijeljina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I move to another subject. This Court has heard evidence, Mr. Ostojic, that the government tried to introduce the institution of commissioners who would be in charge of a number of municipalities. My question to you is: Were you ever a commissioner?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's just that the MPs in the People's Assembly of Republika Srpska could be commissioners on the ground. There was one paper in which the government laid down its decisions appointing some ministers as commissioners as well. However, that decision was varied, and all the ministers were replaced with MPs in the position of commissioners. So maybe you can find a paper in the archive of the government wherein some ministers were appointed commissioners. However, if you look further through the archives of the Assembly, that they were later replaced by MPs in the position of commissioners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you directly receive information from the municipalities? I mean, did you have any direct contact with the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did they ever address you and inform you about what was going on in their municipality?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I had possibly contacts with local media, but not with local authorities; the Ministry of Information did not have such competencies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But even if there was no competence, they might have addressed you and have informed you about what was going on in their municipality.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think that in view of the nature of the jobs, the local authorities would have rather addressed the Prime Minister or the Deputy Prime Minister in charge of local administration, whereas my contacts would have been naturally with the media. My contacts were with local media, if such contacts were technically possible, and if such media were in operation. Because most of the media had very poor technical equipment and many of them were not on the air or not printing most of the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I draw your attention to another document in this bundle which is a document called Supplement 13, which is a handwritten note which is transcribed, and I read from that. It's P653 for the parties. It's dated the 23rd of March, 1992. It is from the president of the Serbian municipality of Kalesija. It is addressed to Minister Ostojic, and it reads, and I quote a part of it: "Political and strategic decisions are being coordinated with the corps command of the 4th Armoured Brigade. I wish you success in the creation of a Serbian State in BH." Do you remember this to be addressed to you?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is addressed to the Serb Democratic Party, attention: Minister Ostojic. I don't remember, however, this reaching me. It was written in the Serb Democratic Party, whereas I didn't hold any position there at the time. At the time I was minister in the coalition government of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Where you say it's addressed to the Serb Democratic Party, are you referring to the stamp at the top?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I don't have that document and seeing this stamp I'm wondering where this was sent. It was sent to the Serb Democratic Party. And this was a time when preparations were being made for holding a referendum without the consent of the Serb people concerning the separation of Bosnia and Herzegovina, the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina, whereas the constitution clearly set out terms for such referenda by any of the ethnic groups within the republic. At that time, I was holding a position of minister in the coalition government of BH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau will put one or more questions to you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ostojic, only one question to put to you. It has to do with the incident of the 26th of July, 1992, during which you were arrested, or stopped --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- on the road at a place called Grbavci on the road from Bijeljina to Pale. And you were stopped, assaulted, by the leader of the Yellow Wasps, Zuco; that's how he was called. Do you remember this episode?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, how could I forget?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You stated that you were threatened by -- with weapons, that you showed your identity card, your papers showing that you were a minister, but that didn't help and that that didn't change the attitude of those you were speaking to. And that eventually the episode or the incident ended well. And you stated that you reported this to the Ministry of Police. What kind of a report did you send?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely what I stated in this paragraph, that I was attacked by that group about which I had known nothing until that moment and that my life for a few seconds hanged by a thread, that it was going to be forever etched in my memory. I also stated that this group was frequently robbing people travelling by bus on that road and that they should be stopped from mistreating and robbing people in the future. And I demanded that all measures be taken, that a state with a rule of law should take. As far as I remember, an intervention by the police indeed followed. This group was stopped, and no such thing happened on that road again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you find it difficult to answer my question, Mr. Ostojic? I'm asking you in which way you reported this to the minister for police.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm having some sort of stage-fright. I'm being rather nervous. I'm sorry. I didn't quite get the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm asking you again in which way did you report this to the ministry or the minister for the interior, of the interior to the minister for police matters?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made a written report to the Ministry of Police demanding that the issue be dealt with, resolved, because it was a huge incident that could have ended tragically for me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you deliver this report in person to the minister?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It went through the channels of regular correspondence between the two ministries.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you mention this incident to the head of the government?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told all the members of the cabinet about it, and as far as I remember the minister of police was acquainted with the incident as well, because as far as I remember I arrived at Pale terrified that night, together with my driver and two passengers, of whom one is a journalist who is now dead. All those people had been with me and witnessed the event which could indeed have tragic consequences because I was nevertheless beaten by that man while I was showing him my ministerial ID.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which were the consequences or what was the follow-up to your report?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police intervened and the group was arrested. I don't know when this happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You didn't try to know whether there was any follow-up, whether people were convicted?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In my view it was enough that the group had been arrested and that such incidents would not repeat, not only to me but to anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just one short follow-up question. You said you don't know when the arrest took place. Could you tell us: Was it, even if you would not know exactly, was it long after the event? Was it just within a couple of days? Was it a couple of months? Could it have been a year? Do you have any idea about approximately how much time it took to have them arrested?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think it was more than ten days after the event, approximately. That group was arrested then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Judge Canivell has one or more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ostojic, please, there is a -- since you told us several times during your testimony that on some questions you were asked were not of your competence. So could you please clearly tell us what exactly was your competence as minister of information?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were three groups of competencies that I had. The first group of competencies was relative to the heading of the ministry or leading the ministry. I was supposed to organise the ministry, its sectors, and report to the Prime Minister with regard to the implementation of all the decisions that the ministry received from either the government or the National Assembly. The second group of competencies was relative to the normative activities of the ministry. The ministry had the task as part of the government to pass laws within its purview. The ministry drafted a law on information in Republika Srpska, the law on electronic media, i.e., the Serbian Radio Television, [indiscernible] radio and television, and also the law on the news agency SRNA, as well as the law which was relative to the ministry itself, its internal organisation within the law on government. The third group of competencies of the ministry was to provide material, financial and technical conditions for the work of the media in Republika Srpska, the founder of which was the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, and by that I mean the Glas Srpski from Banja Luka, the Serbian Radio Television, and the Serbian News Agency. Based on the law on informing, the ministry created the basic preconditions for the functioning of the media in Republika Srpska when it came to their editorial policies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, these functions, you know, to prepare laws, that seems logical, you know, when -- the inception of the ministry. But the report that you were giving to the Prime Minister, these came from the division -- this came from the administration and the parliament of your country, okay. But I'd like to know among your competence, were you also in charge of verifying the facts in order to make sure that the information provided was reliable, reliable to your government, to your leadership, and to your parliament, and also to make sure that the information provided to the media was also reliable? So was this part of your competence to make sure that all of this information was reliable, so to check the information?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If the information arrived from the information services of other state bodies, then the Ministry of Information, with the government, could not check anything. The information services of those other state bodies were responsible for the reliability of that information. If information was to be provided from the government, then the Ministry of Finance was in charge and was responsible for the reliability and accuracy of that information. If we are talking about public information or information that was broadcast by any media in the Republika Srpska, it was the discretionary and right of any journalist in any of the media in Republika Srpska to report professionally in an objective way, and they were responsible for the reliability and accuracy of the information that they broadcast. And in that respect, the Ministry of Information did not feel the need to intervene. Once the law on information was passed, the competencies of the ministry were regulated and so were the responsibilities and the rights of all the media in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. You just told us that when you verified that there were -- when they were -- this information -- you told us about that. So I would like to know something. You told us that you didn't have the means to verify anything, to meet the press, to get information from the media, you know, outside your county, outside Republika Srpska. So how did you eventually manage to find out what -- what was said in the international media? Since you told us that there was some Australian -- you had information on the 50th -- 50-year-old photographs that were seen by the Australian media and you got that information. And you're telling us you were getting no information outside Republika Srpska. So how did you manage to know what was happening in the international media?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry itself did not have technical capabilities to monitor the leading electronic media and world press. However, we managed to help the Serbian Radio Television and the news agency SRNA, and these two had technical capabilities to monitor, record, and download all the relevant information broadcast by the world media. Such information was then forwarded to the president of the republic, to the president of the Assembly, to the Prime Minister, and obviously to the Ministry of Information. In that way, once we provided technical capabilities to the electronic media of Republika Srpska and the news agency, we managed to be informed about some information that was of relevance for Republika Srpska, but not all. We were not technically capable of monitoring 20 channels. We had to make a selection and monitor only those that we considered to be the leading world media. Your Honours, Your Honours, if you will allow me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're not able to directly follow all these electronic media, but you had SRNA, right, and SRNA was the channel through which you got the information that you needed to stay abreast of what had happened and what was reported. And then through you all -- then through you, you distributed the information to all the other bodies of the Republika Srpska. That way, that's how you knew exactly what was said about your country outside your country.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of Information did not distribute such information. I said that SRNA, the news agency, and the Radio Television -- the Serbian Radio Television, that is, of Republika Srpska made press clippings. The agency news of SRNA was received from those who were able to receive that news. And then, to a certain extent, we had an insight into the writing of the world media about Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you said "in a certain way." How exactly did it work? How exactly did you get the information on what was happening outside, you know, after the SRNA -- so you said SRNA was getting the information and how did you get the information afterwards?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SRNA made transcripts of the news and then mailed those transcripts to the state bodies, including the Ministry of Information. And since we were all located in a limited territory, the news was disseminated by means of couriers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now I'd like to ask you something else on another point. You say that when you learned about disinformation that was disseminated throughout the world through the international media, then you organised a press conference. You had one in Belgrade and the other one in Bijeljina. So before convening these two press conferences, what -- how far did you go for -- to verify facts in order to be able to state that what had been given as information was only disinformation? So how -- what did you check on the spot? I mean, you tell us as you've never been to the camps, the collection camps, or the concentration camps, or whatever we may call them, but how did you know exactly -- how did you get the information that was going to be useful for you that -- in order for you to prove that what the media was disseminating was false?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After having received transcripts from SRNA and Serbian Radio Television, the Prime Minister organised a short briefing. I don't know which members of the government were there, but the centre-point of that briefing was myself. In other words, I was tasked to go to Belgrade, and with the help of Tanjug I was supposed to inform all the world media that they could come to Republika Srpska to visit all the corners of Republika Srpska and to see the reality of things on the ground. We were rather disturbed by the individual writings and information carried by the world media. At that briefing, I was tasked by the Prime Minister to share the information that what could be read in the world media was not correct, that we did not have concentration camps, that we had columns of refugees, not only Serbs -- non-Serbs, but Serbs, for example, in Sokolac, Bijeljina, Lopari, in Manjaca, near Banja Luka, and that we also had columns of non-Serb population near Prijedor. The Prime Minister told me at that point that according to the information that the government had, those were not concentration camp. This was just propaganda. Those were just columns of refugees. Based on that information, based on that briefing, I held two press conferences in 1992; one in Belgrade, the other in Bijeljina. I invited all the world media to come to Republika Srpska. And with a huge column of journalists, we came to Bijeljina, and in the grand hall of the Municipal Assembly of Bijeljina we held this press conference. We informed the journalists where they could go, and I told them that they could go anywhere they wanted and that all the state bodies, the government, and the ministries of Republika Srpska were at their disposal. At these two press conferences, I conveyed the positions of my government and the assessment of the government and the information of the government as to what that was all about. The goal was for the world media to visit Republika Srpska unhindered and to provide objective information about the situation in Republika Srpska. Our goal was also to eliminate all -- any misinformation or misconceptions that they might have had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but what you did was not offering facts that could have contradicted what had been printed or written in the international media. I'm asking you if what you did was the following. It's the head of government, through you, who asked you for the press conference, and it was more of a Pavlovian reflex, wasn't it, just a denial of what had been said, without investigating first and foremost whether the information was true, to see -- so it looked like it was more of a deliberate gesture to say: No, this is wrong. But it was not backed on anything, was it, because you really reacted without investigating first and beforehand what had really happened, you know, to get hard evidence that could help you counter what was said.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prime Minister told me that the government had investigated those events after the information that was broadcast and that the government had not been able to establish that the information was correct. He told me that what some world media had published was not correct and he tasked me with conveying that message to the journalists as the position of the government based on the information that the Prime Minister had received from the competent bodies. Second of all, my assessment, as the minister of information, was as following -- as follows. I thought that it would be better and more professional within the sphere of informing. Instead of my word and instead of me telling them we had investigated, although I did say that the state bodies had investigated, and we say this is not correct, these are not camps but columns of refugees. I thought it would be better to say: You're journalists, and we give you an opportunity to visit every single place and see for yourself what the truth is and convey the correct information that will not be checked by us. I'm not briefing you as to what you should write. I am giving you information at this press conference about the position of the government, and I also tell you that you are free to go anywhere you want in Republika Srpska to collect evidence for yourself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understand that. But you say that the Prime Minister had told you that before making this decision to ask you to convene the press conference, you said that the Prime Minister had investigated the fact. But didn't he tell you what the conclusions of the investigation were and what had been actually implemented and so on? I mean, you knew that you were going to be under the -- you know, many questions during the press conference. So, I mean, you could have wanted to get information in order to, you know, have something to say to these journalists. So why was -- that the fact?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. The Prime Minister told me that he had state bodies that had inquired into the matter and that they thought that what the world media wrote was not correct, and that it was my obligation to invite the journalists --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I'm going to rephrase my question maybe. Yes, I was just reading the answer. So it means that you did not know about the results of the investigation carried out by the Prime Minister, that had been asked by the Prime Minister. Then there's another question that I'd like to ask you. You are saying that when -- just before the -- there was the actual opposition -- the conflict, you know, between the three communities in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992, before then you said that a number of media had given information, information that was against the Serbian position, and that there was -- it had been done by paramilitary groups that were not controlled by the government. So if I understood you well, this means that you were not supposed to be held responsible for the fact that this had been published when this media -- when this was actually published by the media. But after this, didn't the media work along the line of the government, along the line of the leadership of Republika Srpska after that? Didn't the media obey?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The media in Republika Srpska - and I am invoking the law on information passed by the Assembly of Republika Srpska upon the proposal of the government based on the draft law of the ministry - were absolutely free. There was no single article in the law that would have enabled the Ministry of Information to control the media. And especially the foreign media. There was no way for me to control the foreign media, nor did it ever occur to me to control them. My only professional task was to allow those media normal work in the territory of Republika Srpska and, given the situation, to provide for their security. And during my term of office, not a single journalist fell victim or casualty in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but my question was the following. After the occupation of the media by these uncontrolled paramilitary groups, after that, didn't the media decide to express itself in line with the government line, actually, you know. In -- so -- so did the media ever express themselves against the line of the government, against the ideas of Republika Srpska? So these -- this media that had been occupied by these people that you call paramilitaries, uncontrolled groups, did they eventually adopt a new line that would be -- did they adopt the line of the government or did they ever express opposition to the government of Republika Srpska? That's what I'd like to know. Did they stick -- after the invasion -- after the fact that the paramilitaries had taken over, after that, did they stick to government line or were they ever able to express themselves against government line?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, in order for me to give you the correct and efficient answer, I have to make sure that I understood your question correctly. I understand that your question actually consists of three subquestions, the first one being the take-over of the media or the occupation of the media in Bosnia and Herzegovina. This was during the coalition government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which was in the second half of 1991. And there were individuals involved in that. Those people were beyond the control of the state organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina during the year 1991, if I understood your question well. And if I did, I believe that I have provided a partial answer to your question. Your second subquestion was whether the media in Republika Srpska could have a different opinion than the government of Republika Srpska. I with state with full responsibility that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm sorry, that was not it. Despite the fact that you had this occupation by uncontrolled elements, the information that was provided after that, after this occupation of the media, was it -- did it align itself in the interest of the SDS line and of Republika Srpska, after this occupation? It's after the occupation that this happened, right?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I understand your question now. Your Honour, like before the occupation of the transmitters, after the occupation of the transmitter and the independent activities on the part of some individuals, the media in Bosnia and Herzegovina did not report in an objective way, and they did not convey the positions of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And let me repeat at this point, let me repeat part of my statement and confirm, like I did yesterday, in response to one of the questions, that the media in Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991 and 1992 were not objective, they were not professional when it came to the national issues of all the three peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And they were particularly biased when it came to the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So outside the question that I didn't ask but that you almost answered, there's the right of media to be free, of course, and to express whatever their opinion is. But as minister of the information, what you noted is that they were biased. You noticed that all these media that expressed themselves that were under the aegis of Republika Srpska were biased, right? You said that there was information that was very partial and that was actually going along the line of the SDS partisans, of the leadership of Republika Srpska. Is that what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's obvious, Your Honour, that we have a language barrier that prevents us from communicating completely, effectively. And I'm afraid that I may be answering an allegation out of context. We're talking about two things: Media in Bosnia and Herzegovina versus media in Republika Srpska. The media in Republika Srpska were not on the SDS line, they were not controlled by the government, and they were absolutely free. Whereas media in Bosnia and Herzegovina were, in my professional assessment and opinion that was formed after 15 years of work in the media, were biased and not objective. So we have to make the distinction between the media in Bosnia and Herzegovina and the media in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. Media could express their own opinion; that's one thing. But still, who -- I had asked you whether you had noted that maybe in -- not deliberately all these media aligned themselves to express the opinion of the SDS and the government who were in power within Republika Srpska. That's my question, not whether they had the right or not. I want to know whether they adopted this position, maybe spontaneously. And I think you told us that they were not -- that they were biased and that they were a bit -- a bit biased, right?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I said that about the media outside of Republika Srpska, that they were biased and not objective. I equally claim that the media in Republika Srpska did not form their reporting chaotically, and they were not following the political line charted by the Serb Democratic Party. They had the absolute professional right held by every journalist to report as they see fit, as long as it was objective and correct. So that was my assessment of the work of the media in Republika Srpska in 1992. Therefore, you could find media in Republika Srpska that held completely different views, journalistic views, from what you could call the official policy of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but could you give me an example of one of this media, paper or maybe a TV programme, that had an opinion that was different from what were the general principles adopted by the SDS and the people who were in power in the government of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for programmes and stories that could be characterised as highly professional and which did not automatically reflect the positions of the authorities, were Radio Banja Luka and Radio Bijeljina, as well as the newspaper Glas, which means voice, of Semberija and Bijeljina. I'm trying off the cuff to find at least two examples in confirmation -- in corroboration of what I said. We could find even more examples if we undertook deeper analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Banja Luka radio, was it totally separate from the Banja Luka television?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, then, what's strange for me is that you told us earlier I think that Glas was a paper that was controlled by the Republika Srpska. So how could a government paper express opinion that would be different from that of the power, the power that was controlling it after all?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I didn't say that the authorities controlled the publication called Glas Srpski. All the control over that newspaper was vested in the laws, the laws on reporting, information, and radio and television. At that time Television Banja Luka did not exist; only Radio Banja Luka existed. At that time, Television Banja Luka was only being equipped to become a separate studio equipped from the resources of Television Sarajevo. The media in Republika Srpska were not controlled. The law did not allow me to control them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CANIVELL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, two very short questions; please short answers as well. Do you read and understand French?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not a word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you read and understand English?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When SRNA prepared clippings, was there a translation with it?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Press clippings were in the Serbian language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those that were submitted to the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also those that were covering foreign media?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was provided to the foreign media and they did not come to the government's attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. I mean -- you said SRNA monitored more or less with their technical facilities the foreign press, that they made clippings, and you said that it was distributed to the Presidency Assembly Ministry of Information. As far as the foreign media were concerned, was that -- how was that translated for you so that you could have access to what was published in the foreign media?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: SRNA had a section employing journalists who knew English, French, German, and, I believe, Spanish. So they took off passages from the foreign press, translated them, and then Serbian translations would be submitted to the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those questions -- for those answers. We'll continue after the break. You'll then be first examined -- you'll then be first examined by counsel for the Prosecution. I'd like to stop the videolink at this very moment. We'd like to see you back in 25 minutes from now. Then once the videolink for the time being -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then I'd like to turn into private session for one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon. Mr. Josse, the session will be extended for 20 minutes. You have time from 11.15 to 12.30. We'll then have a break of 20 minutes, so you have 75 minutes. And the same for you, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I see on my screen that the microphone in -- yes, it's now from my screen, so I take it that we'll now be able to hear you. Mr. Harmon will examine you, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Harmon is counsel for the Prosecution. Please may I direct you to carefully listen to the question and to answer to that question and not to go beyond what was asked to start with.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Ostojic, I would like to direct you to paragraph 49 of your statement in which you say that you were put on an EU list that prohibited you from entering the European Union because you obstructed the implementation of the Dayton Agreement. If we could turn first to tab 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1266, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, tab 15 is in English. I will read to you the relevant parts of it. This is a document that is the High Representative's statements announcing the dismissals of BH Serb officials that was issued on the 30th of June, 2004, and if we turn in the English to the second page, the first full paragraph above the names. Mr. Ostojic, I'm going to read this to you. First -- "First we have in the European Union just announced that we are adding 13 names to our visa ban list for helping ICTY indictees evade justice or otherwise acting in a manner which could obstruct the ICTY in its work. We will be distributing the full list following the press conference, but the following new names are added on this list," and your name is one of the 13 names. Mr. Ostojic, you were banned from travelling in the European Union because of the conclusions of the High Representative that you had obstructed the ICTY in its work. Isn't that the case, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was told that I was banned from travelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And you weren't told a reason why you were banned from travelling, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was precisely this wording: Obstruction to the implementation of the Dayton Agreement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Let's move to a different topic. Mr. Ostojic, let's go to paragraph 23 of your statement. This refers to the 2nd Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly that was held on the 21st of November, 1991, and it refers to an attempt at that time to divide the media. You told us that that proposition ultimately was not accepted?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, the 2nd Session is exhibited already. It is -- portions of that are found in tab 43.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, at the time that you proposed that particular division of the media and the decision --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm referring to page 51 of the text in the English, Your Honour. I'm not going to refer it to Mr. Ostojic. I'm going to relate --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, at the time you proposed that decision, you said that the decision -- "the Assembly of the Serbian People of Bosnia and Herzegovina is duty-bound to ensure objective and truthful education and information dissemination to its people." That's the duty that you imposed upon the -- yourself, is that correct, the dissemination of objective and truthful information?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, if we turn to your statement, your interview -- your interview at page 32, not your statement but your interview, at line 14, you said in your interview, and I quote: "And especially that only correct information can be broadcast because misinformation in times of war creates panic, which means that the journalist must check the source of information." You were also asked questions about that by Judge Canivell, about checking the source of information. Do you, Mr. Ostojic, and did you consider it your responsibility and duty to provide in 1992 truthful and accurate information, both to the people of the Republika Srpska and to the international press?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not my responsibility; it was the responsibility of the media, to proceed from sources of information and to report truthfully and objectively to the people to whom this information was destined.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm asking you, Mr. Ostojic, if you considered it your responsibility when reporting about events, that it was your duty to disseminate truthful and accurate information, both to the people of the Republika Srpska and to the international media.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In view of my area of work, you can take it that it was my responsibility, too, but it was first and foremost the responsibility of reporters and journalists.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, having -- did you in fact, Mr. Ostojic, in fact, always report accurately to the people of the Republika Srpska and to the international media about events that had occurred in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My reporting was through press releases and interviews and communiques and answers to journalists. I myself did not do any reporting. And whenever I appeared before journalists I always tried to speak objectively, truthfully, and correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn to an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we could turn to tab 58.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tab 58 needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1267, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, first off, and I see the document is being put in front of you. This is a document in Cyrillic. Do you recognise your signature at the end of that document?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document that is a proclamation that is dated the 16th of May, 1992. It is from the government of Srpska Republika Bosnia and Herzegovina Ministry of Information. I'm going to read the first two paragraphs and I'd like you to look at it, Mr. Ostojic. "Like ten years ago, the terror equal to genocide is being conducted against the innocent Serbian inhabitants in this war forced upon the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Day in, day out, the hordes of slayers and robbers under the patronage of the fascist authority of the so-called Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina engage in the most brutal actions assaulting the Serbian population at their hearths. Mercilessly the members of the Serbian people are being eliminated and massacred, their property plundered, their villages burned, their cities destroyed, and the monuments of Serbian culture and history shattered." And if we turn, Mr. Ostojic, to the last paragraph in the document, it reads, and I quote: "The Ministry of Information of the government of Srpska Republic Bosnia and Herzegovina provides both the national and international public with an accurate and objective information with the truth about the struggle of the Serbian people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, a struggle for peace, justice, and freedom, and is thus inviting everybody to act in the service of the written word and image." Mr. Ostojic, this proclamation that you issued was of a type that was intended to incite fear and panic amongst the Serbian population. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The third paragraph shows the purpose of this proclamation, that all people of goodwill with their own home-made footage, cameras, documents, and in other ways record all crimes against Serb people so that a documentation be created.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And prior to asking them the objective fact of documenting crimes or acts -- of violent acts committed against the Serb people, the first two paragraphs in this document, I submit to you, Mr. Ostojic, were inflammatory and designed, in part, to incite the Serbian people. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You could, Mr. Ostojic, have merely asked that the people in the Republika Srpska document with their cameras and other forms crimes and violent acts. Why were the first two photographs inserted then, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the first two paragraphs speak about facts on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let's also look at another exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The transcript, Your Honour, is found in tab 44 of the bundle before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, we're going to play a video clip of an interview with you that took place in 1992, and I'd like you to listen to it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "When we're talking about the truth today, is it true that extremists, Muslim extremists, threw Serbian children into the lines yesterday in Sarajevo? "Unfortunately this is true. I can absolutely guarantee this. This picture in the zoo is horrific. In the children's park where generations of Sarajevans of all ethnic groups took their kids out to see the lions and other exotic animals, there in that place, fanatics and butchers are feeding Serbian children to the lions, and that truth will come to light and will reach the world, just like a series of other facts. Like, for example, two days ago in Gorazde, we took out Serbs who were nailed by their hands and feet to rafts or crosses. Or the fact that a raft constructed of Serbian bodies was taken out of the Drina River. I heard that there are many camps in Bosnia where Serbs are still confined today. The last information was that there are 17. In those 17 camps, will 40.000 Serbs are detained, and to date around 6.000 Serbs have been liquidated in a cruel and monstrous way. The largest number of Serbs are in camps today. I heard where many stadiums where camps are located don't have any grass today because the Serbs had to eat grass. They died of hunger at those stadiums. I will give you several examples or, rather, share some information and cite as to where this happened. They included the Gorazde stadium on the right bank of the Drina, the Koseva [phoen] stadium, and the Zetra ice-rink. In Gorazde, our Serb women were forced to walk naked through the city as white slaves. They were hobnailed, tortured, raped in the cruelest manner, and thrown into the Drina. Miserable mothers with small children in their arms were retrieved from the Drina River. Bodies nailed to the cross, to rafts, were retrieved from the Drina River. At this moment, in Gorazde, the Drina is a great dungeon of the Serbian population, and the Drina will -- the Drina will carry away with it a multitude of secrets about the suffering and misfortunate of those Serbs who did not succeed in getting out of Gorazde in time."

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, was that accurate information you were disseminating to the Serbian people and to the international community, that fanatics and butchers were feeding Serbian children to the lions?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This information is what I received from the Ministry of Police in the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Was that information accurate?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Ministry of the Police claimed that the information was accurate, and the population in the neighbourhood of the zoo confirmed that in their statements in the competent service of the Ministry of the Police of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see those statements, Mr. Ostojic, before making that statement?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see the statements of the alleged witnesses who had seen people feeding Serbian children to the lions, before you made that public statement?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I received information from the Ministry of Police of Republika Srpska in the government, and based on that information I issued this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you see, Mr. Ostojic, rafts constructed of Serbian bodies?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, what you were disseminating was the rawest type of propaganda designed, in fact, to incite the Serbian people into fear and into loathing the perpetrators of those alleged crimes. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I absolutely refuse [as interpreted] this allegation. I gave all of my statements based on the relevant state bodies of Republika Srpska, primarily the Ministry of Police which issued information to the government, and then the government tasked the Ministry of Information to convey the message.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, did you ever retract the statements that you made in this particular interview about the feeding of children to lions, construction of -- rafts made out of Serbian bodies, did you ever publicly retract that statement?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Because the information was that something to that effect had happened, and I received information from the Ministry of Police. I did not make this up. I had information from the relevant state body, and the same information had been submitted to the government.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Who, Mr. Ostojic, from the Ministry of Police gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The ministry via an official letter to the government, and I had that information in the government. I suppose you can find that in the archives of the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or in the Ministry of Police of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, my question was: Who was it who gave you that information? Can you identify by name the person from the ministry who gave you that information?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a particular person that brought information. The Ministry of Police of Republika Srpska issued an official document, a dispatch, in order to inform the government of these events. In other words, I used official information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, Mr. Ostojic, that that type of information that you disseminated in that interview would, in fact, cause fear in the minds of Serbian people in the Republika Srpska in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I absolutely disagree. I believe that this was necessary information about the situation on the ground. The information that had previously been verified and established by the relevant bodies of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's change the topic, Mr. Ostojic. Let's talk about the issue of camps, about prisoners, about the detention of civilians in camps that were established by the Republika Srpska. When did that matter become a matter of concern to the government of the Republika Srpska? I'm asking you for an approximate month, date.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could have been either in mid-July or towards the end of July 1992. This is when in -- the world media brought the initial information about some sort of camps existing in Republika Srpska. The information in the world media caused what you're asking me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If Mr. Ostojic could be given extra 1 -- I'm sorry, not extra 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, we have received evidence and the Court has received evidence in this case. The evidence I'm referring to are the minutes of the 5th Session of the Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina that were held on the 10th of June, 1992. At that session, Mr. Ostojic, the Presidency reviewed reports of the international foreign press, and on the 10th of June they instructed Mr. Djeric to have talks on the cost of accommodation and food for refugees and to report to the government on detainees and on proposed measures. Subsequently, Mr. Ostojic, the government session on the 10th of June in which you were in attendance then said that the Ministry of Justice should create or prepare a report on prisoners. I can refer you, if you would look at tab 60, be shown tab 60. Mr. Ostojic, if you take a look at -- these are the minutes of -- this is P582, tab 20 for the record. The minutes of the session indicate in the first paragraph, attendees, that you were present at that meeting, Mr. Ostojic, and on the agenda a number of topics were discussed. And if you turn to agenda item number 7, you will see, Mr. Ostojic, that the Ministry of Justice was to make a report about prisoners. "This report," and I'm quoting, "should pay special attention on the treatment of the civilian population, prisoners of war, accommodation, food, et cetera. The report would be considered by the government after which it would be submitted to the Presidency of the republic." Mr. Ostojic, the government, based on international media reports about what was happening in those camps, became concerned, and you participated, Mr. Ostojic, in this Presidency session where the conclusion was made that the Ministry of Justice make a report about prisoners. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's what the document read, but there is no mention of any camps but of prisoners. Unfortunately, I have a text in English and I'm unable to read.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You should have the B/C/S. If you don't have it -- that's the evidence that the Chamber has received. If we turn -- I'm sorry. Mr. Ostojic, on the 15th of June, the government, according to the government minutes, the government received the report, they considered the report, and -- do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So is it your evidence --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have any documents to that effect before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, the evidence before this Court is that you were in attendance at that meeting. Do you have any recollection, Mr. Ostojic, about what the report about prisoners contained?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. If you could jog my memory with a text. The text that I have before me is in English. From what I've heard, two things are relevant. The Ministry of Justice was tasked with providing information within a certain deadline; and secondly, there are minutes showing who the attendees were. And if the information is received from the Ministry of Justice, the government will undertake certain measures. And this is what I believe is relevant in the text that I have before me and which, I repeat, is in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, put aside the text. I'm asking you to make -- to use your recollection. In June of 1992, the government -- as early as June of 1992, based on international media reports, the government, of which you were a member, was concerned about the accommodation and the treatment of civilians who were being detained by your government. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is. And the government took measures.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It tasked the Ministry of Justice with providing the government with information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, the government of the Republika Srpska was under increasing pressure to open those camps to public view. Correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The government was under the pressure of the media, which said that those were camps, whereas the government spoke about prisoners in the text that I had before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, thereafter, once the matter had reached critical mass, there was an agreement to permit reporters into those camps. Do you remember when that agreement was reached and who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that before the Honourable Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
