utterances.text: Well, say it again --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't think he heard your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You interrupted me. I don't know what to do now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, when did the government decide to permit journalists to enter the camps and who made that decision?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that time, throughout that period, the government never spoke about camps but of prisoners. After the information provided by the Ministry of Justice in June and the first half of July, the conclusion was reached that all the world media should be invited to visit all the places and to see what the real situation on the ground was in order to be able to prepare information. The Ministry of Information carried out their task by having invited all the media to visit Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, before the media was permitted to enter those camps, preparations were made in order to get them into a condition that would appear that those were not concentration camps. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, I have not quite understood your question. Can you repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Prior to the admission of -- into those camps of journalists, steps were made to clean up those camps in order to create an image to the international media that those camps were nothing more than reception centres, not concentration camps. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not correct. The government never did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Are you aware that the -- let's turn to tab 79, please. Tab 79 is Exhibit 1247. Mr. Ostojic, this is an order, urgent order, from General Mladic to prepare Omarska, Trnopolje, Manjaca and all the other prisoner of war camps in the zone of the 1st Corps for visits by the international journalists and the International Red Cross. You are aware, aren't you, Mr. Ostojic, that these camps in fact had to be prepared before the journalists arrived to the camps. You were coordinate -- isn't that correct, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with that. I am not familiar with this document. This is a document of the Main Staff that never reached the government, and I was nothing more but a member of the government. I was not the Prime Minister, who probably was familiar with the document, but I'm not even sure of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, why weren't the journalists permitted into those camps prior to the 3rd of August, 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is not correct that any journalists were prevented from visiting those places before the 3rd of August, 1992 and from staying in Republika Srpska. To the contrary. You can see this in the archive of the government of Republika Srpska, the Serbian Radio Television. Accreditations were issued to numerous journalists from abroad in May, June, and July, who visited Republika Srpska freely and were free to report therefrom. In other words, not for a single moment was any journalist prevented from entering --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did any journalist prior to August the 3rd enter Omarska, Trnopolje, or Manjaca camps, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that. But I know that before the 3rd of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, we're going to look at a video clip.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Video clip 2, please. It needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1268, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: [Voiceover] "Gentlemen, 360 grams of bread per day. If you want to put any questions, this is a minimal value that they received. "They don't beat me and I'm treated as a human being. I'm familiar with the Geneva Conventions, and physical and oppressive measures have not been applied. "Every other day to the camp for prisoners."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I seem to have lost my image of Mr. Ostojic, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that will come back. We've forgotten to assign a number to tab 44, which was the interview with Mr. Ostojic. Mr. Registrar, that would be --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1269, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P1269. Then the last clip played would need a number as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Clip 2, Your Honours, was assigned P1268.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I see that. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, those scenes of abundance were created for the journalists' benefit in order to deceive them as to the lack of food that had priorly -- that had previously been available to the inmates. And you were aware of that, weren't you, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I really can't say what this is all about. All I could see was a kitchen of some sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Those were images that were taken at the Manjaca camp, Mr. Ostojic. I want to show you some photographs, Mr. Ostojic, starting with tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Registrar in Belgrade, I'm going to be going through a series of pictures. I'm going to be doing this very quickly, so if you would follow my lead, please, starting at tab 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, let's look at the photograph -- paragraph 220 -- tab 20, and then if you could look at the photograph, Mr. Ostojic, at tab 21.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1270, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tab 22, also look at that, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1271, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tab 23, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1272, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The next tab, 26 -- I'm sorry, tab 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That needs a number, 27.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we jump from tab 23 to tab 27?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1273, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tab 28, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1274.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, finally, tab 29, that needs a number as well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1275.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, those are images of people who came out of the camps at Omarska, Trnopolje, and Omarska [sic]. Do these photographs -- are you familiar with those photographs, Mr. Ostojic? Have you seen them before?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not familiar with these photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You told us earlier, Mr. Ostojic, that the -- there was some monitoring of the international press. These photographs, Mr. Ostojic, received considerable attention in the international press following the visit of the international journalists to Omarska, Trnopolje, Manjaca. Is it your evidence, Mr. Ostojic, that you never saw those until you have been shown those photographs today, never seen them before?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not see them in this form, but I did see a -- one photo, I believe, on CNN. I'll try and find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did it appear to you, Mr. Ostojic, from the photo that you saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, would you give an opportunity --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to Mr. Ostojic to find the photograph he said he saw at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Tab 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Tab 25, Your Honour, was not exhibited. But if we could get a number on tab 25, that would be fine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1276, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: My question to you, Mr. Ostojic, of the many emaciated images of people -- strike that. Of the many images I have shown you of emaciated people who came out of those camps, did you ever see any such images, Mr. Ostojic, following the visits of the international journalists to Manjaca, Omarska, Trnopolje?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you which photo I remember. I remember having seen probably on CNN.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, listen to my question --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And as for the others --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you ever see photographs of emaciated persons who had been in Omarska, Trnopolje, or Manjaca, the type of which I've shown you today? Did you ever see those photographs or similar photographs disseminated in the international press following the visits of the reporters and the journalists to those camps, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, save for the one that I just showed you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do these photographs shock you, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Is it the first time you've seen such photographs?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw similar photographs, but not from these lands. And I find all such photographs extremely harrowing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, let's turn to paragraph 43 of your statement, where you say you have never visited Susica camp. Mr. Ostojic, you visited Susica camp on approximately the 2nd of September, 1992, along with members of a mission to Bosnia from the conference on security and cooperation in Europe. Does that refresh your recollection, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I cannot remember accompanying any sort of mission to a camp like that. I cannot recollect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I'm going to ask that a photograph be placed on the monitor in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: For the benefit of the registrar's representative, it's 00456976.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could you -- do you see that photograph, Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do we find it in our bundle?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's in your Court bundle, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry. These will be disseminated, Your Honour. This is a photograph, colour photograph that bears an ERN number at the lower right-hand corner, 00456976.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, the man in the middle of that image wearing a suit with his arms crossed is you, isn't it, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot recognise myself there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Could this have a number, this particular image?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It looks to me as though this man is shorter.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1276, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, let me try to refresh your recollection again, Mr. Ostojic. If you take a look at image --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You are asking for this particular image to be -- get a number. In fact, it would be P876.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There's another image, Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I appreciate that my learned friend needs to go quickly, but the answer the witness gave which is on a transcript was basically obscured by an attempt to get the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It is on the transcript. He said, "It looks to me as if this man is shorter."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's on the transcript. I heard that and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it appears on the transcript. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, we're going to look to another image. And for the registrar's benefit if you would turn to 00456978. Mr. Ostojic, look at that image, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, this is an image also that needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That would be P1277, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, prior to your visit in Susica camp, an effort was made to hide the inmates and therefore hide the belongings so representatives from the conference on security and cooperation in Europe would not see them. The image I'm showing you now, Mr. Ostojic, is a photograph taken of clothes and articles of prisoners that were concealed behind boxes. Does that refresh your recollection, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I simply have no recollection of ever seeing this with my own eyes or visiting myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, we're going to turn to a different topic, and that is found in paragraph 31 of your interview where you said that you disagreed with the allegation that had been put to you that the SDS party in the period of late 1991 and throughout 1992 increasingly came to control the media outlets in the territory of the Republika Srpska. If we turn, Mr. Ostojic, to tab 67, this is P64, P65, Treanor 14, tab 213, P583, tab 216. Mr. Ostojic, the document that is being shown to you is an excerpt from the 22nd Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly held on the 23rd and 24th of November, 1992. Mr. Ostojic, this is found at page 32 of the English, and, Mr. Ostojic, you should have the excerpt in front of you. It is 27 of the B/C/S, and I'm going to quote you, Mr. Ostojic. "Mr. President" -- the second sentence I'll quote. "The magazine Srpksa Vojska published at the Serb army headquarters aims at showing that the information system of the Serb nation is developing in the direction defined by the SDS and directed by the National Assembly and its executive organs." Those are your words, Mr. Ostojic, in November of 1992. Do you remember making them?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember saying this, but I see that it's written that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, do you remember that at the end of July going to Banja Luka and summoning a meeting of the editors of all the Krajina media, Glas, Radio and TV Banja Luka, and other radio stations? The topic of the meeting was to decide guidelines for the general direction of all Serbian media in Bosnian Krajina. And the intention of that meeting was to orient the editors in the direction of the ideology of the SDS. Do you remember that meeting, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the meeting. It's possible that I had a meeting, one in a series of countless meetings I had with journalists, including various interviews. But I cannot remember precisely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, Mr. Harmon, one question in between. Mr. Ostojic, the magazine Srpska Vojska, was that a government-edited magazine or was it a privately owned and -- I'm trying to find out whether this is a specific government organ or whether it was part of the independent press.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not a newspaper. It is not an independent medium, nor a privately owned medium, nor is it a government-controlled medium. It was prepared by a publishing section of the Main Staff of the Serb army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: In paragraph 8, or page 8, paragraph 34 of your statement you were asked questions about local attempts to control media content, and you said and you were shown evidence of such a situation in the municipality of Petrovac. And you considered that to be an isolated case. Let us turn, first of all, to tab 80.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It needs an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1278, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document, tab 80, Mr. Ostojic, is a -- from Kljuc municipality, the Crisis Staff of the Kljuc Municipal Assembly. It's May of 1992, and I direct your attention, Mr. Ostojic, to the section that deals above VI. This isn't paginated, but, Your Honour, in English it's -- the last four digits are 7665. And this document, and I will quote it to you, Mr. Ostojic. "The work of Radio Kljuc will be carried out according to Crisis Staff instructions and the execution of tasks will be the responsibility of," and it names two people, "whose task is to determine the internal organisation and the entire work of Radio Kljuc." Mr. Ostojic, let's turn to tab 82, which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Also would need a number, Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, this needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This document, Mr. Ostojic, is dated the 29th of May, 1992. It's a decision of the Crisis Staff of the municipality of Ilidza, and in the decision, item 1, the Ilidza Radio Television network is founded. And if you turn to item 6, for its work the board is responsible to the Crisis Staff, respectively to the Serb municipality of Ilidza. And if you turn to tab 83, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document that needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1280, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is dated the 8th of June, from Sanski Most municipality. This is a -- it says in item 1: The political and information department of the Crisis Staff of the SDS is hereby informed. Vlado Vrkes is appointed head of the department. It names another person as a deputy head. They shall form a department encompassing the staff of the radio station, political commissioners from the field, and it goes on. The Court has heard evidence in P186, an exhibit, that Mr. Vrkes was in charge of implementing the ideas of the SDS leadership at the level of the republic, regional, and municipality levels. Do these examples I've shown you illustrate that Bosanski Petrovac was not an isolated case?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sense in which Radio Bosanski Petrovac is concerned in the question, I still maintain that it was an exception because it was their editorial policy. In this case, the document mentions only the establishment of the Radio Television.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, we're going to change topics, because one of -- I want to direct you to paragraph 36 of your statement when you were asked about a statement that was heard on the radio in Foca on the 9th of April, 1992. You denied making the statement, saying that your father had died on the 25th of March, and that you stayed in your family's house for a longer period of time, according to Orthodox customs. When did your -- when did you arrive in your family's home following the death of your father, what date?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 24th of March, in the evening, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: How long did you stay at your family's home?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stayed until, according to the Orthodox custom, I performed the rite on the 40th day after the death of my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Do I --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first according to the custom is funeral, on the day of the funeral --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm not interested -- at this point, Mr. Ostojic, I'm interested in dates. How many days did you stay at your family's home in the Foca municipality following the death of your father?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's actually a village around 25 kilometres away from Foca, maybe more. I stayed until almost the end of April, until the 40th day after the death of my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, in paragraph 36 you said that, and I quote: "I was physically not able to state on the radio after Foca had fallen into Serb hands that the township was Serbian," and it goes on. What did you mean by "physically not able to state on the radio"?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I was in that village, that is as remote from Foca as it says here. Because I was visiting with my mother, who is 90 years old and who was alone. Because I have no other family, no sister, no brother, so I had to take care of my mother during that time and I had to stay at her house.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you at any time while you were in Foca, from your family residence or other location in Foca, make any communications via the radio? Did you make any reports what about what was happening in Foca or did you have the means to do so?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was when I arrived at Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: While you were in Foca, Mr. Ostojic, did you make reports about the situation in Foca and what was happening in Foca, through any media form whatsoever, including the radio?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that once when I went to call on my uncle in that period, and when I took him to Celebici to my family home, there were some journalists who turned up there and I gave them a statement. It was not a report; it was just a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When was that, Mr. Ostojic, approximately, what date?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it could have been at the time of the 40-day rite, around the 20th of April, let's say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, we're going to go through a series of exhibits very quickly. If we could go to tab 48, please, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This needs a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1281, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, this is an English text. It is from the Radio -- Belgrade Radio network. It is dated the 8th of April, 1992, and it says: "Velibor Ostojic report." And it discusses in this what was happening in the municipality of Foca. Let me turn to a different document, Mr. Ostojic, tab 50, if you could look at that. Mr. Ostojic --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This needs a number. I'm sorry, Mr. Registrar, this needs a number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1282, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, this is two reports, there are two. One is found on the first page of the English, one is found on the second page. The first of the page, this is 14th of April, 1992, Belgrade Radio Network, Velibor Ostojic report from Foca. That's at 1500 hours. If we turn the page, we see the same date, same news media, at 1300 hours Velibor Ostojic report from Foca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me try to find it, Mr. Harmon, I have some problems. Yes, the first one was 48, the second one was 50, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: There are two reports in 50, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I was looking at the next one, which is not the right one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then -- Your Honour, I need to go into private session on this particular document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm going to refer --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, this is a document that is dated the 23rd of April, 1992, Belgrade Radio. It's Velibor Ostojic, report from Foca. And it says, Mr. Ostojic, that the Serbian people of the Foca region are indignant of yesterday's reporting by some agencies on the supposed genocide of Muslim people. Such news is really only lies and untruths. We categorically reject such things. No one is touching or endangering the Serb -- the civilian population or their property." Mr. Ostojic, these documents -- these reports from Foca, do they refresh your recollection, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I take the greatest exception to this extraordinarily long question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The witness cannot deal with these unless each and every extract is put to him, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps we first approach it in a more general way. Mr. Ostojic, what Mr. Harmon did is he gave a large number of -- he put a large number of documents to you, which all suggest that your activity at that time was not focussing on family issues, but that you were at least involved, rather intensively, in reporting on what happened in Foca and that you have met the representatives of international organisations. And he does so, I take it, because in your statement you said: I could not have given a certain radio statement because I was with my family and at least at 25 kilometres from Foca. Would you, in view of the number of documents Mr. Harmon has put to you, would you comment on your possibility or impossibility to make even one statement in a radio programme?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when I said that I was physically unable to give the statement that was quoted in my statement in paragraph 36 on page 9 of the statement under discussion, I meant that statement, that I was physically unable to give it. And I suppose that it regarded the time when I was in my family home. And as for these reports, I said that I remembered being in Foca on the 20th of April, around that date, at my uncle's home. And there is a telephone in my home in Celebici. And I talked to late Koljevic, and he told me that he would come to Foca on the 19th, 20th, or the 21st, and that I should be there to take his car with him to Pale, to the seat of the government of Republika Srpska. That's when I met with Mr. Koljevic at my uncle's home, and that's where the mission was. And I remember it well. And then a crew from Radio Belgrade was on the same spot. They wanted a statement from me that they turned into reports, whereas in fact I gave them statements about what I was able to find out while being at my uncle's home. And I gave a statement about what was going on in Foca in those days. So those are the statements that I gave to Radio Belgrade, a crew of which found me at my uncle's house, which was in the suburbs, and that much is true. However, before or after that day when I was expecting to meet Mr. Koljevic, what I stated earlier about being physically unable to give such statements, that regards the period up to the 15th of April when I wasn't in Foca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, last question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, in respect of paragraph 40 of your statement, you were confronted with allegations that had been made in this court that you attended a meeting on approximately the 10th of May. Mr. Deronjic reported the ethnic cleansing of the municipality of the Bratunac. You said that you denied being present at that meeting and you deny making a -- such a statement. And you asserted that blue was not the colour of Serbs. Let me direct you to tab 57, Mr. Ostojic. 57, Mr. Ostojic, is an exhibit. This is P65, Treanor 12, tab 127 and 129. This is the 16th Session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly. Mr. Ostojic, you are quoted in this. I'm going to refer you to -- in the B/C/S language to page 22 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's empty in our binders, Mr. Harmon, but if you would please then slowly quote of this document which is in evidence already.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You have it -- Mr. Ostojic, you have it. I'm going to refer you to page 22 in the B/C/S. It has the last four digits of the ERN 7737. Mr. Ostojic, the quotation, Mr. Ostojic, I'm going to be directing your attention to reads as follows: "Thus I appeal and plead that we get started working in that fashion. The third thing as far as realisation of strategic goals is concerned, that they have been presented here in rather general terms, these goals may be developed further and presented as variations or as including a set of mutually complimentary subgoals. However, here is one point of view. We have the idea and the realisation of this map of ours, and I do believe I was the first to start drawing the map and they are an idea on which the diplomacy has to work, but they, the borders, will be drawn and established only when we make them a fact. I believe that peace with Alija can only be achieved by war." It goes on to say that: "Europe and diplomatic circles will recognise something that is under our control." And it -- that session Mr. Krajisnik says, and I'm referring page 49 of the English. And, Mr. Ostojic, for your benefit it is found at page 36 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm afraid, Mr. Ostojic neither has it. Could you take it -- I take it you are talking about the colour. Could you come to your point and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour, ask two questions instead of just one because I can't frame it any other way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's start with the first one and then we'll --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, the fact is that you were quite familiar with and used maps that depicted Serb-occupied territory in the colour blue, contrary to what you suggest in your statement to this Tribunal. Isn't that the case?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not the case. I have nothing before me. I have empty tabs, empty pages. I don't have a single document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, forget for one moment about the tabs. Are you familiar or would you agree, that's the question put to you by Mr. Harmon, that on maps often the colour blue was used to indicate what portion of a territory was occupied by or controlled by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wouldn't agree, Your Honour. This was not exclusively in that colour. It was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your last part of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wouldn't agree that this was exclusively in the colour blue, that the so-called "occupied territories" were only in blue. It is possible that those were the boundaries of municipalities with the Serb population. Now whether they were marked in red, white, blue, blue and red, blue and white, I really wouldn't know. This varied from one case to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, I would highly appreciate it if you do not change my question while giving an answer. I never said "exclusively." I said "often the colour blue was used." Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would say that oftentimes colour blue was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Then one final point I need to direct his attention to, Your Honour, in this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, but that is really then is the last one, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It will be, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik at that same session, Mr. Ostojic, in describing the strategic objectives, and particularly the first strategic objectives, said, and I quote, I'm referring to page 49 of the English version: "That is why it would be good, my dear gentlemen, to take care to leave enough space for division. I shall be a bit immodest. Do not hold it against me. We once placed the option on our agenda of making a map, and should anyone offer us 80 per cent of the territory we would not be able to work out a partition. Even if there were -- even if we were deciding on how to do a partition because it is very difficult, we are everywhere. That is why I propose that we also adopt a conclusion, that a group is to be established, a working-group, and a commission which would say: Here, this is the map. I like Mr. Ostojic's maps most, and everything on them is blue." Mr. Ostojic, you did attend the meeting in Glogova on the 10th of May. You did use a map that depicted Serb territories, and those territories were coloured blue, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not attend the meeting on the 10th of May in Glogova because on the 10th of May I was in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I meant Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, thank you very much for the indulgence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, just to clarify the latter. Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Harmon made a mistake when he said you did attend the meeting in Glogova on the 10th of May and that you used the map, et cetera. You said: "No, I did not attend the meeting on the 10th of May in Glogova" because you were in Pale. Did you attend that meeting in Pale of which Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. On the 10th of May I was in Pale in the government, and I was drafting the law on the Ministry of Information for the following session of the government which was to take place on the 12th of May in Banja Luka. And already on the 11th of May I was on my way to Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. We'll have a break. We'll have it as briefly as possible. Mr. Registrar, would it be possible to resume at five minutes to 1.00. Yes, we'll resume at five minutes to 1.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, you'll now be examined by Mr. Josse, counsel for the Defence. And, Mr. Harmon, I'm drawing your attention to the fact that on page 47, line 14, I think your question, at least as it appears in the transcript is a Presidency session in which Mr. Ostojic would have been present, where I think as a matter of fact that you were then referring to a government session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that's how I, at least, thought that Mr. Ostojic would have understood that question, but it's not a major issue, I think. Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The first thing I'd like to ask you about is as follows. This Court has heard evidence from an English academic called Dr. Mark Thompson, who was called as a purported expert on the media of your country during the war that this case involves. Have you ever heard of such a man?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He asserts, and it's fair to say that he reads and understands your language, that the SDS in Bosnia successfully brought media outlets under its control. And using these -- I beg your pardon, and using those media as megaphones sought to convince Serbs that their very existence was threatened by Muslim and Croat genocidal tendencies fueled by ambitions for independence. What do you say about that conclusion from the expert, Dr. Thompson?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is erroneous, biased, and incorrect. The SDS did not have its own media, and Republika Srpska, through the laws that it passed, showed that it did not have any desire to control the media. And of course it did not have any influence on the editorial policy of the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He went on to say, and I quote: "That far from performing the usual watch-dog role of media in a democracy, the media outlets under actual or effective SDS control were used to block, express and marginalise information and opinion that dissented from the SDS orthodoxy. There was wholesale support in this effort from influential outlets in Serbia, in particular RTS, Serbian state broadcast network." What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. Would you please repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. I'll actually break this quote up. Firstly, he did: "that far from performing the usual watch-dog role of media in a democracy, the media outlets under actual or effective SDS control were used to block, express, and marginalise information and opinion that dissented from SDS orthodoxy." That was what Dr. Thompson said. What's your view about that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion is entirely different. Having spent long years working in the media, I give myself right to provide the following evaluation. The media in Republika Srpska were independent and free in the expression of their journalistic activity. This can be proven by the law on information of Republika Srpska. Secondly, the media in Republika Srpska, which were established sometime in mid-1992 as the media of Republika Srpska, published all information regardless of the political position of those who appeared in the news. And they reported on all the events in their programmes. In other words, this claim is not correct. It is far-fetched. And what I am talking about can be found in the archives of either the electronic media or the written media. And you can see that the media Republika Srpska were very broad coverage of all different information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: He went on to say that: "There was wholesale support in this effort from influential media outlets in Serbia, in particular RTS, the Serbian state broadcast network." In other words, he says that RTS supported your efforts in marginalising information and opinion that dissented from SDS orthodoxy. What do you say about the Serbian involvement?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that this allegation is not correct. The media in Republika Srpska and by the nature of things, if we are talking about the Radio Television of Serbia, the equivalent would be the Serbian Radio Television. In other words, the Serbian Radio Television was an independent medium and it was under nobody's control, under nobody's influence, under no other media influence. In other words, it performed its information function independently and under no influences. And if you're talking about the information activity of the television in Republika Srpska and the Radio Television of Serbia, in one breath would be a very unprofessional way of looking at the activity of both media. It is a fact that journalists of the Radio Television of Serbia, like all the other journalists representing all the other international media, had an opportunity to report from Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Now, he gave eight areas that in his opinion demonstrated the SDS leadership's determination to control media outlets in the Republika Srpska. I'm going to go through these one by one. If you could comment on each of these briefly, I'd be grateful. A number have been dealt with in your statement. Firstly, he said: "Attacks on and efforts to divide Radio Television Sarajevo, RTVSA."

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are documents to that effect, speaking of broad public discussion amongst all the members of the coalition government and all the parties that constituted the coalition government of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is widely known that the Radio Television of Sarajevo did not report objectively and did not report professionally, and therefore it should have been reformed and reorganised by introducing new broadcasting channels that would be much better at expressing the needs of certain groups in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Secondly, he relied on the establishment of control over RTVSA transmitters. I know that's something you have dealt with in your statement. Is there anything else you want to add about that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The organised activities with regard to the establishment of control over RTVSA transmitters did not exist. But, as I've already said, there were some isolated individual cases. In two cases, individuals acted in that way with regard to the transmitter on Mount Kozara, and a transmitter which was not as a matter of fact a transmitter but a repeater at Ciganiste near Doboj. However, the interventions of these individuals also happened in Majevica, Trovrh and Pljesevica. These individual interventions were very soon eliminated.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Next he relied on attacks on the premises and staff of Oslobodjenje newspaper.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such case. I don't have information showing that there were attacks on the Oslobodjenje newspaper, and I don't know what period he is referring to when he says that. And I believe that this is an allegation which has been taken out of the context of the overall developments at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: His fourth point was the SDS establishing control of Glas newspaper based in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is a malicious statement which can be refuted by irrefutable proof about the activity of the government of Republika Srpska during the time. This activity was aimed at turning a little-developed regional paper into a daily that would be able to perform its information activity. Secondly, I am not aware of any activity on the part of the SDS involving that medium, but I claim with full responsibility that every activity of the government aimed at empowering that paper called Glas and raising that paper to the level of a daily. Before they received the government's assistance, Glas was not a daily, it was a periodical. After an extensive assistance by the government of Republika Srpska, and the assistance was of financial and material nature, that paper became a daily. There was no activity on the part of the SDS there. The activity was aimed at turning a periodical paper into a daily that would cover a much larger area, and all the technical and financial support was given with that goal in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The fifth point was establishing control of the TVSA studio in Banja Luka. Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no such studio. At the beginning of 1992, until the important laws were passed in Republika Srpska which dealt with information and electronic media in Republika Srpska, there was an information and technical centre there of the Radio Television Sarajevo which was not capable of producing independent information. They could just process the recorded material and send it via link to the Radio Television Sarajevo studio in Sarajevo. And it was there where it was decided whether any of that material would be broadcast or not. Very often the RTV Sarajevo would reject any such material, and there were a lot of complaints about that addressed at me as minister in the coalition government. The government of Republika Srpska, i.e., its Ministry of Information, took measures in May and June in order to turn this information and technical centre into a television centre which would be able to broadcast programmes independently. At the beginning it could broadcast only to the extent covered by the transmitter on Mount Kozara.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Number 6, establishing control over Radio Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Radio Banja Luka, until the year 1992, was a local town, a radio, which was incorporated into the so-called joint programme of the radio stations of Bosnia and Herzegovina. As for its editorial policy, as well as of the other local stations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, it was decided in the central editorial programme board of Radio Sarajevo. It was only when the normative and material activity was undertaken by the government of Republika Srpska, just like in the case of the information and technical centre in Banja Luka, which happened in the second half of 1992, did Radio Banja Luka receive technical and material capabilities to be able to broadcast its programmes independently. And it did start broadcasting independently in keeping with the law on Radio Television of Republika Srpska, which at the moment was known as the Serbian Radio Television, Banja Luka studio. The law on information, which was implemented as of mid-June, unequivocally regulated the relationship between the founder, which was the National Assembly of Republika Srpska, and Radio Banja Luka. In editorial terms, Radio Banja Luka was an independent medium, i.e., the journalists were independent in editing their programmes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The seventh point is a rather general one and one that, for the most part, you dealt with, but I'll put it to you nonetheless. Establishment of SRNA, establishment of SRT, and printed media in Serbia-controlled areas. Is there anything specific you'd like to say about that that you haven't already in the course of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would just like to add to that that the government of Republika Srpska, through its Ministry of Information, managed to change the Banja Luka Glas from an insignificant paper into a daily. And this is all that the government of Republika Srpska did. And I've told you everything else about the media. SRNA was a news agency which was also founded in order to provide agency news in a profession manner. This news was news not only by the Radio Television of Republika Srpska, but its news was taken over by a number of international agencies, which can be seen from the daily bulletin of the news agency SRNA. And you can see in those bulletins which well-known international agencies used the services of SRNA, which means that those services were professional. The law on the -- of the open market says that if the news of one agency is not up to the standard of another agency, the latter will not take that news over. Because there is payment involved, there is money involved. The fact that the agency news of SRNA were -- was taken over by powerful international news agencies shows to prove that SRNA worked in a professional and objective way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Dr. Thompson's eighth and final point, again something you have dealt with and indeed you've just been asked about by my learned friend, Mr. Harmon, was the issuance of instructions from SDS and Republika Srpska bodies to secure control of media entities. Presumably you stick by your assertion that that basically did not happen?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. First of all, I would like to stick to what I have already said, but I would like to confirm this and illustrate it. The competencies of the minister of information was to talk freely to the journalists, and the Ministry of Information of Republika Srpska never resorted to such an administrative measure to organise briefings for the journalists. This is a well-known administrative issue in the sphere of information or, as it is stated here, instruction. In journalism, it is very difficult to establish something that you might call as instructing journalists. Journalism requires regulation and it implies that journalists are independent in the performance of their duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You were asked specifically in your interview with a particular broadcast by Radio Petrovac, and that was read out to you and is dealt with at paragraph 34 of your statement. I'm going to read to you what you said about that during the course of your interview, because it's rather fuller than the answer we see at paragraph 34. You said: "I want to say three things. First, at the general level, I want to say there was no editorial policy in the media in Republika Srpska that aimed at inspiring or influencing any individual crimes, and you can see that from the documents of the government and the Ministry of Information. Number two, there was no information and propaganda planned for such a thing. And three, the quote from Radio Petrovac does not show any aggressive policy or war-mongering. It's simply an assessment of the situation but rather clumsily done. It speaks about the defence of one's own people against the enemy that's either surrounding them or that may be somewhere on the horizon. There is a feeling that the enemy is coming. I see it as a call to be vigilant, but I don't really know about this quotation. To conclude, the Radio Petrovac example is rather an isolated incident, an exception, and it's not a system or a plan." Do you stick by that answer that you gave during the course of your interview? Perhaps you didn't catch my question at the end of the quotation, Mr. Ostojic. The question was: Do you stick by that quotation that I have just read out that you gave during the course of your interview with a Legal Officer of this Chamber?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was a comment to the allegations about Radio Petrovac. I don't have that in that same form in the statement that is before me under item 34. This is a shortened statement. Since, things being as they are, I would like to say the following. And this could be seen -- and one can say this was an isolated case with regard to the story of the editorial policy of a local media. Second of all, Radio Petrovac, under technological terms, was a medium under minor influence and minor range. And third of all, I cannot accept this case as an example of the global activity of the media in Republika Srpska. I stick by my statement that this was an isolated case.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Do you have any recollection of visiting Prijedor in August of 1992 accompanied by a large group of foreign journalists?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This was the group that I took from Belgrade, and I held two press conferences, one in Belgrade and the other one in Bijeljina. And I was also almost a personal escort to all those media. The column was about -- almost a kilometre long. I was there to encourage them and to enable them a direct access to that area because I felt amongst many of them personal fear. They were afraid that they would not be able to pass through, and some of these journalists told me: Mr. Minister, we will go if you come along. And I took them to Prijedor, and they could see that they could move about freely and that they could use that trip for producing information such as they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]. Shall I try now? I think the problem was I had turned my microphone off and then had to turn it back on again. I'm sorry. We had a technical problem, Mr. Ostojic. I'm now going to ask you about paragraph 45 of your witness statement. You were asked some questions about this by the learned Judge, Judge Hanoteau. Did you discuss this incident, the incident of your being stopped and attacked on the Bijeljina-Pale road with either Mr. Mandic or Mr. Stanisic? The question is: Did you directly discuss this incident with either Momcilo Mandic or Mico Stanisic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I didn't. I was rather excited and shattered, and as soon as I arrived in my office at the government I drafted a written report about the case for the Ministry of Police and I asked them to intervene.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: This Chamber has heard some hearsay evidence, by that I mean not a first-hand account, an account from a person who had spoken to another person, where it was suggested that as you were taken from the car you said something along the lines of: Zvornik would become a, and I quote, "dead end." Do you have any recollection of saying that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The -- this would not have made any sense. There was no context for me to say that. I was never in a position to say anything else to that group but to identify myself as a minister on his way from Bijeljina to Pale. I absolutely reject any possibility that I could have said something to that effect, and I cannot collect statements from the eye-witnesses who were there who can prove that, and maybe you can even find people who were on the bus who were astonished by the way that group treated me and threatened me. And at that moment, I didn't even know what attacked me. I described the event which can be seen in the archives of the government. I mentioned a group that had beaten me heavily. It was only subsequently at the end when they were about to let me go that one of them introduced himself as Commander Zuca, and this is the only information that I had about the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is a suggestion that at the same roadblock, at around about the same time, not necessarily the same day, the same period, the same group of Yellow Wasps waved Momcilo Mandic through the roadblock, whereas they stopped you. Did you hear anything about that? And, second question, can you give any explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not know about that group until they intercepted me and put so much pressure on me. To say that they mistreated me is an understatement, and of course I did not hear that another member of the cabinet was intercepted either before or after I was. Of course I heard something like that happened, although not to Mr. Mandic but Minister Lajic, minister for communications, around that time. Not the same day though.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And finally on this topic, do you have any idea who was charged by the minister of the interior with cleaning up the Yellow Wasps?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. But I was informed that the Ministry of Police took urgent steps to clear out the Yellow Wasps and, as I said before and if I remember correctly, that was done very quickly within several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In your statement at paragraph 19 you say, and I quote: "The relationship between me and Mr. Krajisnik was very official." What do you mean by the words "very official"?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I meant business-like, first and foremost, professional and business-like. We did our respective jobs within the powers vested in us.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: You would say, would you not, that when Mr. Krajisnik was president of the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina, he felt that solutions should be sought that would ensure equality between ethnic groups and that predisposition was clear in the way he conducted parliamentary business. Do you agree with that statement?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely. And I think that Mr. Krajisnik himself said as much on many occasions during fierce debates in the Assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And his style of leadership over the multi-party, multi-ethnic and very complex Assembly on very complex circumstances demonstrated precisely his capacity for rational thinking that led me to make this assessment. He was the Speaker of an Assembly where he had many times to appease very fierce discussions and contributions that sometimes went out of control.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you would contrast the air of tolerance, dialogue, and democratic decision-making that existed within that Assembly to the situation that was occurring at the same time in the cabinet and Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Would you agree with that assertion?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And when I said that I, too, had a very business-like and official relationship with Mr. Krajisnik, I also meant by that that Mr. Krajisnik, as Speaker of the Assembly, never interfered with my line of work unless that was justified by his own work. And I also wanted to raise one more thing that I remember, now you ask me this. The sessions of the then-Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and even the sessions of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and even the People's Assembly of BH, were broadcast at the time - that was the latter part of 1991 and 1992 - and there was a great contrast between the style of the Speaker of the Assembly, which exuded tolerance. Although, by its very nature the Assembly gives greater freedom of expression than in the Presidency, on one hand, and the work of the Presidency where members of the Presidency would sometimes even walk out because they were dissatisfied with the way the president of the Presidency was conducting the deliberations. In the government where I worked, government sessions were often interrupted as well in order to resume dialogue and try to conduct the session in a more or less normal way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In paragraph 23 of your statement, you talk about efforts that you made to try and reform the central media in Bosnia and Herzegovina because of the way that you believe the Serbian ethnic group was being ignored. You talk about proposed amendments which had the support of the Croatian Democratic Union but did not win a majority. What sort of reforms did you propose at that time?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in this interview, in broader terms than expressed in this paragraph, I managed to say that on the 18th of November, 1990, when the coalition government, composed of SDA, SDS, and HDZ, came into power, it inherited a sort of cemented situation in the media, the leading media, of Bosnia and Herzegovina, primarily Radio Television Sarajevo and Oslobodjenje newspaper. The previous authorities of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina made up of members of the League of Communists of Bosnia and Herzegovina had cemented this law on Radio Television Sarajevo, the law on information, and others, and appointed its own members to the posts such as editors-in-chief, programming, directors of television stations and leading newspapers. And the situation we inherited from the previous authorities was such that the new authorities could do nothing to reform organisationally or in terms of programming the Radio Television Sarajevo or the Oslobodjenje newspaper. So based on consultations held within the cabinet and within the Ministry of Information that was made up of representatives of all three ethnic groups, some reforms were proposed to reform the media, to open new television channels under the umbrella of Radio Television Sarajevo for which all the technical conditions existed, and to reform the management that in professional terms did not meet the requirements of the future reforming government made up of these three parties that had won the elections on the 18th of November that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: In terms of this pre-war period, I'd like to ask you about a passage in your interview, so it's not in the statement you have in front of you. It's at page 22 for the benefit of those that have this interview. This interview, Mr. Ostojic, though conducted in your language with the aid of an interpreter, has never been transcribed into your language. So I will have to read it to you. You were asked by Ms. Karsten, who was asking questions on behalf of the Chamber, about the take-over of power in municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina and a reference you had made to a plan among the Bosnian Serb leadership. And you said: "I think that there was a general trend of the demands from the grassroots or on the ground that some decentralisation of local government should be carried out. All the three ethnic groups dealt with this issue and discussed how to reorganise government at the municipal level, so this issue ended up at the government session. I think the Cutileiro Plan reflected this idea of all three local groups towards decentralisation and reorganisation of local government." Could you expand upon that at all, please?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a plan. It was a general public debate. It was an across-the-board demand of all ethnic groups at a grassroot level to perform a decentralisation of local authorities on the republican level, because not a single ethnic group was happy with the way municipalities were delineated by the former communist powers. Therefore, members of the government who were Muslims, Muslim representatives, tabled proposals to reform the Janja municipality and to separate it from Bijeljina municipality, to separate Dobrotin or Dobrocic from Jajce municipality at the request of Croats, of the Croat population. Serb population at local level also had its own demands. And all of them were subsumed into one general need to perform decentralisation, including changes in local structure to grant maximum rights to municipalities and to rule out the possibility of out-voting between ethnic groups. So this was a completely justified request from grassroot level by all ethnic groups because municipalities had been formed prior to 1990 -- over that long period prior to that year, 1990, in a completely artificial manner. So this was discussed by the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and one of its conclusions was that the relevant ministry, the ministry for local self-administration, should use all these proposals from the local level as a basis for making a proposal of its own concerning the way municipalities should be structured in the future and the way in which they would be the -- the power would be decentralised.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I want to now take you to the period after May of 1992 and ask you about the members of the Presidency at that time, that is after May of 1992, in the Republic of Srpska. Would you agree with my proposition that the only members of the Presidency at that time were Mr. Karadzic, Mr. Koljevic, and Mrs. Plavsic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without any legislation to support various arguments, we can discuss this issue in one way or another. We can look at it in different ways. However, the legislation of Republika Srpska stipulated that members of the Presidency of Republika Srpska are precisely those that you named: The president of the Serbian Democratic Party or the president of Republika Srpska, that is Mr. Karadzic, late Mr. Koljevic, and Mrs. Plavsic. According to the legislation that prevailed in Republika Srpska, they were members of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, could you invite the witness to further expand on where he said: You could look -- "you can discuss this issue in one way or another." Could you explain to us what you meant by that?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: So, Mr. Ostojic, the learned Judge is asking you to explain what you meant by the words "we can discuss this issue in one way or another." What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that in cases where the legislation is not clear as to who the Presidency's members are, so I agree with what you said, the members of the Presidency were Karadzic, late Mr. Koljevic, and Mrs. Plavsic, because legislation did stipulate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you understand -- as far as you were concerned, were either Mr. Krajisnik or Mr. Djeric members of that Presidency in 1992?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's neither what I understood nor was I ever told that they were members of the Presidency. The Presidency took its decisions, and the relevant, the competent, state authorities had the duty to implement those decisions. So I repeat, in my understanding, the members of the Presidency were Mr. Karadzic, late Mr. Koljevic, and Mrs. Plavsic. There is a decree, I believe, according to which the members of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina became members of the Presidency of Republika Srpska, because they were elected by the people to be representatives of one ethnic community in the highest state body in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: When you say "that neither what I understood nor was I ever told," you're talking about 1992? You didn't understand that to be the position in 1992 when you were in Pale as a member of a government nor were you told it by any government or party functionary? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, if you would allow me, I would like to go back for just a couple of lines. Mr. Ostojic, you started your answer by saying: "Without any legislation to support various arguments, we can discuss this issue in one way or another. We can look at it in different ways. However, the legislation of Republika Srpska stipulated that members of the Presidency of Republika Srpska are precisely those that you named." Your answer suggests that there is another way of looking at it which is not supported by any legislation. And then you said: "However, the legislation stipulated that these were the members." Now, could you please explain to us how you could look at it, although there is no legislative support for that, how you could look at it the other way. Because that's what clearly is suggested in the beginning of your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that introduction that I made was an incautious comment on the question by Mr. Josse. So, if you allow me, I'll correct my testimony to eliminate this incautious comment of the question and to focus strictly on the question itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the answer would be this: The members of the Presidency were strictly those that we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, Mr. Ostojic, what you said is part of your evidence. I do understand that you say it's incautious. What I would like to know, and that's my question to you, what did you have in mind when you made that, as you said, incautious introduction to your answer? What was the other way of looking at it you had in mind?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if it is not known at this moment that there existed legislation that stipulates strictly who the members of the Presidency of Republika Srpska were, that's what I meant. And that's why I said immediately that such legislation does exist, and it stipulated clearly who the members of the Presidency of Republika Srpska were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I asked you -- well, I have to establish that -- that was just -- Mr. Josse, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this a different way. When you said: "We can discuss the issue in one way or another," did you mean anything by that particular remark or was it simply a turn of phrase?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't mean anything in particular. I just made an introduction as a turn of phrase, indeed, for the answer that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The next topic I want to ask you about briefly only is in relation to what you understood as a member of the government to be Mr. Krajisnik's power. And in particular -- perhaps I'll do it like this. You were asked by the learned Judge, Judge Canivell, what your competencies were. After the war broke out in Republika Srpska, what did you understand Mr. Krajisnik's competencies to be?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I understood that Mr. Krajisnik, just all the other elected MPs from the ranks of the Serbian people, had a term of office as representatives of the Serbian people and that his competencies were those implied in the post to which he was elected by the MPs as representatives of the Serbian people; namely, to be what the MPs elected him as and they continued to see him as president of the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about his influence on the government, as you understood it? Tell the Chamber about that.

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think, considering that I was a member of cabinet and also a member of the coalition government in 1991 when Mr. Krajisnik was Speaker of the Parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and since I was also a member of the government of Republika Srpska in the following year, when Mr. Krajisnik was elected president of the People's Assembly of the Serbian people, based on the comparison of his style in leading both parliaments, I can say that the approach of Mr. Krajisnik remained unchanged. In other words, apart from professional contacts I did not feel that he had any stronger influence that he might have had on the government of Republika Srpska than he had on the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina from his position, and that what prompted me to say that our relationship was very official. By that I meant very professional, within the limits of our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: What about his ability to control in any way either the VRS or the MUP of the Republika Srpska after the war had begun? Are you able to comment upon that at all?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to the MUP of Republika Srpska, the MUP of Republika Srpska, in organisational terms, was located as a department of the government. I could not see or observe a different relationship between that ministry and him than between the Ministry of Information and himself. And as for the VRS, I can't tell you anything about -- without any reliability because it was out of the purview of any ministry within the government. And at the end, let me say that the influence that any MP in the National Assembly of Republika Srpska might have had on the government and Mr. Krajisnik as the Speaker of the Parliament was within the norms and established relationship between the National Assembly and the government of Republika Srpska provided for by the law. The government was the executive body of Republika Srpska and any subordination was within the legislative norms.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm about to run out of time, Mr. Ostojic, and there's one last thing I want to ask you before I sit down and that is this. It is right, as I think you stated in a preliminary telephone conversation that you had with a Legal Officer of the Chamber, that you did provide a witness statement to the Defence of Mr. Krajisnik. The answer to that is yes, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But it's right, isn't it, that that --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I interrupted you. But it's right, isn't it, that that statement was given as long ago as September of the year 2000 --

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I gave my statement as a potential witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ostojic, when Mr. Josse speaks, would you please refrain from speaking at the same time, because otherwise the interpreters cannot follow us. Mr. Josse, you're putting to the witness that the statement was given a long time ago. You mentioned September of the year 2000. Please continue from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Would you accept that, Mr. Ostojic, that the statement that you gave to those acting for Mr. Krajisnik at that time was given in the year 2000, in the month of September?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And it's right that you have given no statement since then?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I must admit that where I intended to be very strict on timing, and I only got permission for 20 minutes, I notice that where I wanted, as a matter of fact, Mr. Harmon to stop at -- after exactly 75 minutes, when I said "last question," that took another couple of minutes, which delayed the time a little bit, the break, and also puts you in a disadvantage of a couple of minutes. So if there would be any very urgent matter, and with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I try and present a cross-examination in a reasonably cohesive and palatable way. I deliberately ended with those particular questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Clearly an advocate needs to know when he is time-barred exactly how long he's got. I was told I had to end 20 minutes after 1.45. That is what I've done. In short, Your Honour, I need to know in advance, not when I sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I apologise. Perhaps I should have told you. I said, I think, two things. I gave a time schedule, and I indicated that both parties would have the same time and that would result in -- and then in practice matters developed slightly different from that. And I just didn't want to be unfair to you in this respect. If you say: I'd rather then leave it at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, thank you for explaining that. I don't think I could be -- I could sensibly continue this cross-examination for another two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is one question from -- remaining from the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Ostojic, please, yesterday I'm sure you remember you were shown a document that made reference to Variants A and B dated the December 19, 1991. And you were also shown a clipping published in Slobodna, the title of which was: "Serbs, Get Ready for War."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps for Belgrade that is at tab 49.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: Tab 49, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was dated March 12, 1992. Do you remember this, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: VELIBOR OSTOJIC [Resumed]
